questions.stem: The portal log for one day shows 12,400 submissions. The failure rule fired on 318 of them, and none of those requests had previously succeeded. How many successful submissions could a rule that watches only failures never see?

options.text: All 12,082 submissions that succeeded, since no failure was recorded
Only the 318 that failed, because a success leaves no trace to watch
options.misconception: believes a successful request leaves no evidence at all

options.text: The 318 failures, because those are the only events with a signal
options.misconception: counts only the events that the rule actually fired on

options.text: None, because a success is the same as a failure with no error
options.misconception: treats every request as if it produced an error

questions.explanation: A failure-watching rule sees only requests that failed, so all 12,082 successful submissions are invisible to it, including malicious ones that happened to work. No error is not evidence of good behaviour.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a literal-match rule can be moved off
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a literal rule can be evaded without changing intent.
questions.stem: Rule 22 alerts on the literal text 'drop table' in a zoning application comment. Explain how a requester could keep the same intent while never producing that exact text.

answer.exemplar: A literal rule compares characters, so it can be evaded by changing the spelling, spacing, case, punctuation or encoding of the payload without changing the intent. Splitting the phrase across a line break, changing the case of one letter, or inserting a comment marker between the words all produce text the rule does not match. The rule must normalise and decode before it compares, or key on structure rather than on one exact spelling.

questions.explanation: A literal rule compares one exact spelling, so changing case, spacing or encoding moves a request past it while the intent survives. Normalising the text before comparing closes that gap.
questions.hint: Ask how many spellings the rule accepts.

questions.hint: Compare each variant character by character.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a detection rule actually keys on
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a threshold rule keys on and what it omits.
questions.stem: The memo describes rule 31 as alerting when the same account submits more than 40 applications in one hour. Explain what that rule actually keys on, and what it does not tell the reviewer.

answer.exemplar: The rule counts events per account over a fixed window, so it keys on submission volume attributed to one account, not on what the applications contain, who submitted them, or whether the account holder is human. A reviewer reading the alert therefore knows that a threshold was crossed and nothing more: the count may reflect an automated tool, a shared office account, or a genuine flood, and the rule cannot distinguish those cases on its own.

questions.explanation: The rule counts submissions per account in an hour, so it keys on volume attributed to one account and says nothing about content or identity. A threshold crossing is a prompt to look, not a finding.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule can and cannot see.

questions.stem: The portal records application fields, submission times and login events, but it does not record process-level activity on the permit server itself. Explain what this gap means for the rules and for an investigation afterwards.

answer.exemplar: Every rule built on this feed is limited to what the application layer emits, so activity on the host below it is invisible: a program started outside the portal, a scheduled task, or a change to a permit file produces no application record at all. questions.stem: The rule for a normal number of permit status changes per week was learned from last year's traffic, and the department has since moved most inspections to a mobile workflow that writes changes twice as often. Explain what happens to the rule.

answer.exemplar: The rule compares this week's activity with a baseline learned when changes were recorded half as often, so nearly every ordinary week now lands beyond the threshold and the alerts are dominated by routine mobile workflow entries. questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a legitimate boundary change on a learned rule.

stimulus.body: Rule 19 flags zoning applications whose parcel size in square metres is far from the learned average. The city annexed a new district in April, and applications from the annexed area are routinely larger because the parcels there are larger.

questions.stem: Given this excerpt, what does the annexation do to rule 19's usefulness?

options.text: Nothing, because the rule measures parcel size and annexation does not alter it
options.misconception: believes a policy change cannot affect measured values

options.text: Legitimate large-parcel applications now flood the queue as false alerts
The rule becomes more accurate, since it now sees a wider variety of parcels
options.misconception: assumes more data always improves a baseline

options.text: The rule stops firing, since no application now matches the old average
options.misconception: assumes an out-of-date average silences the rule

questions.explanation: A learned average of parcel size predates the annexation, so ordinary applications from the new district sit far from it and generate false alerts. The rule must be retrained on current data.
questions.hint: Ask whether the world changed, not the rule.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a learned rule sits close to the boundary

questions.stem: A learned rule marks an application unusual when its values fall far from the learned centre. Stage one: a legitimate change raised every applicant's typical value, so almost all traffic now sits beyond the old boundary. Stage two: the team asks whether a genuine outlier will now be caught. What is the answer?

options.text: Yes, more reliably, because the rule now sees more variety
options.misconception: believes a stale baseline improves detection

options.text: Yes, because the outlier is further from the centre than before
options.misconception: measures distance without counting how many normal items also cross

options.text: No, because the rule has stopped evaluating applications
options.misconception: assumes a flooded rule stops working

options.text: Not usefully, because the outlier arrives buried in routine alerts

questions.explanation: When almost all traffic sits beyond the boundary, a genuine outlier is only marginally further out, so it is buried among routine alerts. Only the noise grew.
questions.hint: Ask how many normal items also cross the line.

questions.topic: What a detection rule actually keys on
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a field-pattern rule keys on and what alerts do not prove.
questions.stem: Rule 76 fires when the string 'permit' appears in a field that usually contains a parcel number. Explain what this rule actually keys on, and what a reviewer should not conclude from an alert.

answer.exemplar: The rule keys on a character string appearing in a field that is supposed to hold something else entirely, so it is really watching for a category confusion rather than for anything about permits or applicants. A reviewer should not conclude that a permit was sought, that anyone was authorised, or that the parcel is in question: the alert only says that the letters appeared where a number was expected, and a parcel reference such as 'permit-lot-9' or a pasted note would trigger it as readily as a real request.

questions.explanation: The rule keys on a string appearing in a field that should hold a number, so it watches for a category mismatch. An alert does not show that a permit was sought or anyone was authorised.
questions.hint: Ask what field the pattern was read from.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The gap left by what is not collected
questions.learningObjective: Explain the investigative limit of an application's own records.
questions.stem: The city can query the permit portal's own records, the web server's request logs and the firewall's session logs. Describe the investigative value that the permit portal's own records cannot provide on their own.

answer.exemplar: The portal's records describe only the requests that the application handled and the fields it stored, so on their own they cannot show what happened around those requests. They cannot say which client made the call, what the server did in response at the network level, or whether the request ever left the building, because that context lives in the server and firewall logs. For an investigator, the portal records are necessary but not sufficient, and the missing context is the part that distinguishes a bored resident from a scripted run.

questions.explanation: Portal records cover only handled requests and stored fields, so client, network and outcome context lives in the other logs. Assuming application data describes the whole event is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask what the portal never sees.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What legitimate change does to a learned baseline
questions.learningObjective: Recommend the treatment of a rule after a legitimate change.
questions.stem: The rule for normal submission size was learned from the old paper-plus-web workflow, and the city has since replaced it with a fully electronic system that sends larger files. Explain what a team should do about the rule and why.

answer.exemplar: The learned baseline describes the file sizes of a workflow that no longer exists, so nearly every legitimate application now sits outside it and the rule's alerts are almost all noise. Leaving the rule as it is would consume analyst time and train people to ignore the channel. The right response is to retire or retrain it against current traffic, and to treat a sustained flood of similar alerts after a known change as a baseline problem to be fixed rather than a run of separate incidents.

questions.explanation: The baseline describes a workflow that no longer exists, so ordinary applications sit outside it and the alerts become noise. The rule should be retrained or retired after a known change.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change was planned.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a detection rule actually keys on
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a digit-pattern rule keys on and what alerts do not prove.
questions.stem: The memo describes rule 44 as firing when a submitted application contains the digit sequence '1999'. Explain what that rule keys on, and why a reviewer should be careful about reading too much into an alert.

answer.exemplar: The rule keys on a four-digit character run appearing anywhere in the submitted text, so it can fire on a reference number, a year, a survey figure or a stray phone number rather than on anything meaningful about the application. A reviewer who reads the alert as evidence that the application concerns a property from 1999 is being led by the digits rather than by the data, and should instead open the record, find the exact field and the surrounding context, and judge whether the run is meaningful there.

questions.explanation: The rule keys on a four-digit run appearing anywhere in the text, so it can fire on a year or a reference rather than on anything meaningful. A reviewer must find the field and its context first.
questions.hint: Ask where in the text the digits appear.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The blind spot left by keying on failures
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the submissions a failure-only rule never inspects.
questions.stem: During a quiet week the permit portal processed 9,000 submissions and 260 of them failed. The failure rule was the only rule running. How many submissions could that rule not have examined at all?
questions.explanation: The rule examines only failures, so it never examined the other 8,740 submissions, almost the whole week. A failure-only rule set therefore works from a small minority of traffic.
questions.hint: Subtract the failures from the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: One spelling of a sequence, and the other one
questions.learningObjective: Compare the hits a substring rule produces on two comments.
questions.stem: A rule looks for the four characters 'sale' in a field. Stage one: a comment reads 'sale of land' and matches. Stage two: another reads 'wholesale' and also matches, because the rule does not require word boundaries. How many of the two comments trigger the rule, and what does that show?

options.text: Only the first, because the second does not contain the word sale
options.misconception: believes a literal rule checks word boundaries

options.text: Only the second, because the rule skips the common word sale
options.misconception: invents an exception for frequent words

options.text: Neither, since a rule must match whole words to be valid
options.misconception: insists that every rule must use word boundaries

options.text: Both, and the rule therefore reports matches that are not the word it names

questions.explanation: A literal rule matches the character run wherever it appears, so both comments trigger it and the second is a false hit. The rule needs word boundaries or a stricter pattern.
